Quick sizing guide

The fit you want

Your shin guards should:

Cover most of your shin without restricting your knee.

Have the foot section covering the top of your foot and ankle securely.

Stay in place when you kick, check kicks, and move around.

Feel snug but not painfully tight around your calf.

Have minimal rotation/sliding during training.

Too small: exposed shin near the knee or ankle, foot protection doesn't cover enough, uncomfortable pressure.

Too large: guard slides down, rotates sideways, or interferes with your knee when checking kicks.

If you're between sizes, I'd generally choose the smaller size for a snug Muay Thai fit, provided the shin and foot are adequately covered.

Cover your shin from just below the knee to the top of the foot.

What I'd actually do

If you're a beginner:
I'd choose a good mid-sized gym, rather than automatically going to Tiger. You want enough students to find suitable training partners, but not 30+ people fighting for a trainer's attention.

Good examples include:

Sinbi Muay Thai — probably my strongest all-round recommendation for traditional Muay Thai.

Rattachai Muay Thai Gym — smaller, highly regarded option in Chalong.

Phuket Fight Club — good if you want a broader combat-sports environment.

Sutai Muay Thai Gym Camp Shop — good smaller alternative around Bang Tao.

Yak Yai Muay Thai — interesting smaller-gym option with an unusually large number of current reviews.

If you're going for 1–2 weeks and want the full "Muay Thai Thailand" experience: a big camp makes more sense. The social environment and huge variety of training partners are genuinely valuable.

If you're staying a month or longer: I'd lean smaller/mid-sized. The difference in individual attention compounds over hundreds of rounds.

If you're an experienced fighter: don't choose based on fame at all. Choose based on who will actually coach you, the quality of the fight team, sparring partners at your level, and whether the gym actively gets fighters bouts.

One particularly important point: don't confuse "small" with "better." A tiny gym can have mediocre coaching. A large camp can have excellent coaches. The sweet spot is often a respected gym that's big enough to have a real fight team but small enough that the trainers know who you are.

Generally the best combination of drier weather, lower humidity, and manageable heat.

Much nicer for doing two training sessions a day.

Good conditions for recovery days at the beach or exploring.

Phuket's Andaman-side dry/travel season runs roughly November–April.

🥈 November–December

Also excellent. November is when the wetter period starts giving way to the better Andaman conditions, although November can still have some significant rain. For example, Phuket recorded about 237 mm of rain in November 2025. 
Department of Land Transport

🥵 March–April

Still very good for training, but hotter. If you're planning two hard sessions every day, the heat can make the experience substantially tougher. April is the hottest part of the year in Thailand. 
Tourism Authority of Thailand

🌧️ May–October

I'd choose this period mainly if you need to travel then or want potentially cheaper/quieter conditions. Phuket's wet/monsoon period is roughly mid-May through mid-October, and the Andaman side gets considerably more rain.

+1

The upside is that you can absolutely still train Muay Thai—rain doesn't shut the gyms down. You just have less reliable beach/island weather.
